title: How a World War I Crackdown Predicted ICE
gist: Sam Thielman reviews Derf Backderf's graphic novel The Dissidents, set around The Masses magazine during WWI, arguing Woodrow Wilson's Espionage and Sedition Acts, Bureau of Cartoons and the vigilante American Protective League are eerie precursors to today's mass-deportation politics and ICE/DHS enforcement—and that history shows such repression can recede.

insights.claim: After the Espionage Act of 1917 the U.S. Postal Service refused to deliver The Masses for allegedly interfering with conscription, and the magazine shut down amid prosecutions, reconstituting as the milder Liberator.
insights.speaker: Sam Thielman
insights.so_what: Historical precedent for state use of distribution chokepoints to suppress media in wartime.
insights.locator: The life of The Masses was short

insights.claim: Woodrow Wilson signed the Sedition Act of 1918 and the Espionage Act, which the reviewer says still plagues U.S. civil libertarians, and created a Bureau of Cartoons to censor editorial cartoonists.
insights.speaker: Sam Thielman
insights.so_what: Wartime legal tools for speech restriction remain on the books and can be revived.
insights.locator: Wilson signed the notorious Sedition Act

insights.claim: The American Protective League, a Wilson-approved vigilante group operating under color of law, raided businesses and, over three days in 1918, conducted draft-card checks across New York City and arrested suspected dodgers.
insights.speaker: Sam Thielman
insights.so_what: Shows how executive-sanctioned enforcement can expand quickly in wartime.

insights.claim: The Wall Street Journal ran an unbylined front-page editorial on April 6, 1917 warning militant pacifists 'there is no shortage of hemp or lamp-posts,' which the reviewer likens to today's press disciplining less hawkish voices during the Iran war.
insights.speaker: Sam Thielman
insights.so_what: Media consensus pressure during wars can crowd out dissenting analysis.
insights.quote: there is no shortage of hemp or lamp-posts
insights.locator: The rest of the press seemed

insights.claim: Thielman argues the WWI-era crackdown is eerily similar to the 2024 Republican National Convention's 'mass deportation now' signs and the work of ICE, Homeland Security Investigations and Customs and Border Patrol.
insights.speaker: Sam Thielman
insights.so_what: Frames current immigration enforcement as part of a recurring authoritarian cycle—a societal/political risk lens.
insights.locator: All of it seems eerily similar

insights.claim: The review opens by describing 1916 America in terms that mirror the present: an autocrat in the White House, a paramilitary force loyal only to the executive, plutocrats allied with white nationalists, and prosecutions of dissent as treason.
insights.speaker: Sam Thielman
insights.so_what: Signals how commentators are framing US democratic backsliding risk.
insights.locator: An unambiguous autocrat holds the White House.

insights.claim: WWI cultural pressure forced renaming of German-sounding comics, such as The Katzenjammer Kids becoming The Shenanigan Kids.
insights.speaker: Sam Thielman
insights.so_what: Illustrates wartime nationalist pressure on media and brands.

insights.claim: The reviewer finds relief in the parallels: U.S. repression has been bad before and was later curbed for long periods.
insights.speaker: Sam Thielman
insights.so_what: Suggests mean reversion in political repression cycles.
insights.quote: they’ve been bad before and gotten better (and worse)
insights.locator: Undergirding the eeriness of its parallels
